desc: survivesVerification used filter(Boolean), so a truthy-malformed vote ({} / {real:null}) stayed in the denominator as a refutation and could silently drop a real blocker — the guard failed OPEN on invalid input instead of closed

buildgate classified with `=== 'mutating'` (narrow allowlist) while the rails path fail-closed-CHECKS any unrecognized 'other' structured tool — a secondary gate covered a NARROWER input surface than the primary gate it shadows, so a novel mutator name bypassed it

the resolveOwning(payload, undefined) fallback branch (pathless mutator, no explicit root) had no committed test because every test supplied the short-circuiting root arg — an untested defensive branch a reviewer repeatedly flagged as unproven
mergeHooks used (hooks.event ?? []).filter — ?? defaults only null/undefined, so a valid-JSON but non-array event value (object/string/number) threw an uncaught TypeError and crashed the scaffolder

isAdlcHook used an unanchored substring regex, so a user hook whose command merely CONTAINED an adlc basename (run-adlc-audit.mjs) was misclassified as ours and silently dropped — an identity match not anchored to a boundary destroyed user data

the doc honesty smoke asserted a required string is PRESENT but not that a contradictory overclaim is ABSENT, so a future edit could keep 'buildgate is advisory' and add 'the in-session hook is unbypassable' and still pass — presence-only checks don't enforce honesty

changedFiles and gitDiff scan git output without -z or quotepath disabled, so non-ASCII paths are C-quoted and the returned string is not the authoritative path a scanner needs.
rail-freeze checkRailEdits consumes the quoted non-authoritative changed-file list, so editing a frozen rail path with a non-ASCII filename is never matched and the gate passes silently.
spec-lint heading and criteria scanning has no fenced-code awareness, so a heading-like line inside an example fence desyncs section state and real acceptance criteria are silently dropped.
the read-only shell classifier is anchored at start but not end, so a whitelisted read verb chained before a mutating command via semicolon lets a rail write evade the enforcing gate.

the shell mutation allowlist omits network-fetch-to-file tools and the reactive git-diff backstop is blind to gitignored trust-root files, allowing a fetch to overwrite the active-ticket trust root undetected.

the surface-intersection changed-files derivation requires literal a/ and b/ diff prefixes, so an adversarial diff using alternate apply-compatible prefixes is classified out of scope and the fuzzer skips an in-surface mutation.
the documented bare file_path fallback does not exist, so a write target under an unrecognized container shape is invisible to scope-violation detection rather than conservatively surfaced.

When a CLI advisory check gains a new mode flag, sibling copies of the same check embedded in other plugins or integrations (e.g. multiple editor Stop-hook implementations that each independently shell out to the same underlying command) are easy to miss; a repo-wide grep for the exact shelled-out command is needed to find every caller, not just the ones the ticket scope happened to name.

Tightening a shared library function's tolerance semantics (moving from an unscoped 'anywhere' tolerance to a scoped positional tolerance) silently changes behavior for every existing caller of that function, not just the caller the change was written for; each existing call site needs its own comment update and its own regression test for the new boundary condition, or the behavior change ships unreviewed and untested at those sites.

A new CLI flag that is unit-tested only against the underlying library function in isolation has no coverage for the actual argument-parsing and flag-to-option wiring in the binary; a flipped negation, a typo in the flag name, or a dropped option pass-through would ship undetected unless a test spawns the real binary end to end.

An advisory session-end hook that reports a security-relevant signal (evidence-chain tamper detection) is often the actual bug being fixed by a change, yet has no direct test coverage of its own; downstream test files assert only on a stubbed spawn's canned return value, never on the literal arguments passed to the spawn, so a reverted fix would leave every existing test green.

A chain-only (unkeyed hash-linkage) integrity check cannot distinguish a wholesale-forged, entirely-unsigned ledger from an honest ledger whose history genuinely predates a security feature's adoption, since forging a chain needs no secret. Extending a lenient/tolerant mode to a new caller that treats a clean chain-only pass as a tamper-detection signal makes that caller inherit this limit, even where the underlying guarantee was previously relied on only by callers with an independent defense-in-depth check. Document this limit explicitly wherever the lenient mode is offered.

A test that calls, in-process, a function which spawns a sibling CLI from ambient PATH is not hermetic: it resolves whatever binary the runner's PATH happens to hold. It can pass on a dev machine via a stale global install, pass under the suite runner via its bin-dir PATH prepend, and fail only in a third context that runs the same test files with neither. Such tests must pin PATH to the workspace-local bin themselves.

A test asserting that a directory mtime advances between two writes performed microseconds apart races kernel timestamp-tick granularity: on Linux, file timestamps are cached per tick, so consecutive operations can share an mtime and the assertion flakes, while macOS passes by filesystem timing luck. Rewind the mtime to a fixed past instant with utimes before the first read so the later write's advance is guaranteed observable.

The reviewer-directed-comment gate and rails-guard both transitively depend on @adlc/core for changedFiles, resolveBase, and git enumeration, but packages/core is not registered as a trust root anywhere. A PR could weaken changedFiles to silently omit a changed path, defeating every gate that reads its output, without touching any currently protected file. Remediation: add packages/core (or its git.mjs/index.mjs exports specifically) to the trust-root list, CODEOWNERS, and the tier classifier.

The rails-guard job runs npm install without --ignore-scripts, unlike the test job. A candidate postinstall in any workspace package.json (none trust-root tier by package prefix alone) could shim node/npm onto GITHUB_PATH before rail-freeze and every gate in that job run, making them all report success without executing. Remediation: add --ignore-scripts to the install step and classify workspace lifecycle-script paths as trust-root tier.

CLASSIFICATION_PHRASE is a lexical denylist, not a semantic classifier: it matches only enumerated English dismissal phrases. Cross-model review reproduced a new bypassing synonym in four separate rounds (invalid, false positive, out of scope, and more). A structural alternative would flag any review-process reference by default and require it to match a narrow, audited neutral-reference allowlist instead of matching against a dismissal denylist.
Empty or whitespace bind fields are treated as bound so resume-auth can clear a deny that should stay unbound
Ensure deny marker rewrites when an existing marker is unreadable, clobbering consumed or host-repaired state
Quarantine moves corrupt self-named deny markers so cooling reentry fail-opens instead of denying
Consume accepts a missing or empty consumer session id and clears open deny for third sessions
Whitespace-padded session ids bypass same-session consume checks that only trim for emptiness
Mutation gate fail-opens denier sticky deny when current session id is missing empty or padded
Deny marker writer accepts whitespace-padded session ids that the mutation gate treats as unusable breaking denier sticky after consume

A hand-written validator and a shipped JSON schema that claim to enforce the same contract disagree: the validator accepts unknown keys the schema forbids, and the schema accepts kind and domain pairings the validator rejects.
A hard upper bound that a configuration may only lower is never exercised with a configuration that tries to raise it, so removing the clamp leaves every test green.
A test guard that signals misuse by throwing is placed beneath production code that catches every throw and turns it into an ordinary recorded outcome, so the guard cannot fail a test.
Locating the main checkout by requiring the git common directory to have a conventional name rejects valid repository layouts such as submodules and separate git directories.
A configuration check that the contract says runs before any local state is read is performed only after other files have already been read and parsed.

An adapter contract named in the spec is implemented with a different signature, dropping its timeout and revision parameters and the identity-mismatch rule, so follow-up adapters target the wrong interface.
Counting keyed by attacker-influenced strings into a plain object lets inherited prototype member names corrupt or silently drop entries.
A per-item allowlist of visible fields is validated but never applied, so every item receives the full input set.
Documentation for an exit code groups a failure that happens after an external call with failures that happen before it, and claims nothing was sent.
A row added to an ordered reference table is inserted out of order.
A test that a mode performs no writes runs only in an environment where a write was impossible anyway, so it passes regardless of the behaviour it names.
An allowlist step meant to select the declared fields from collected state instead rejects any collected field that is not declared, so a configuration declaring a subset can validate yet never run.

Every fixture keeps the base branch at the branch point, so a computation meant to start from the merge-base is indistinguishable from one that starts at the base tip and the merge-base step is untested.
A field meant to record a value the external system reported is filled with the requested value when the system reported nothing, so the record claims an observation that never happened.
A write to a path inside a repository-controlled directory follows symbolic links, so a cloned repository can redirect the write to a file outside it.
A validator and the evaluator of the same rule disagree on which keys apply to each variant, so a rule can validate and then be evaluated by a branch that silently never matches.
A function's return value omits a field its documented contract requires, and the caller recomputes it separately, so the contract and the implementation drift apart unnoticed.

A fix that changed a rejection into silent filtering left the specification and its acceptance criterion describing the old rejection, so the criterion's test now asserts the opposite of what the criterion says.
A parser that splits machine output on a delimiter assumes a free-text field cannot contain that delimiter, so a legal value containing it is truncated and misclassified.
A tool option that changes how a measurement is counted was chosen in code while the contract names only the command, so the recorded signal silently differs from what the contract describes.
A command-line flag whose absence makes the parser produce invalid numbers is never exercised by a test, so removing it would leave the suite green.
A guard with two alternative refusal conditions is tested only with inputs that trip one of them, so the other condition can be deleted without any test failing.
A symbolic reference is trusted as soon as it can be read, without checking that its target exists, so a dangling reference skips the fallback and produces a misleading diagnosis.
Most named secret patterns have no sample in the tests, including ones too short for the generic fallback to catch, so narrowing those patterns would let real secrets through unnoticed.
A range check is tested only at its upper bound, so the lower bound can be removed or tightened without any test failing.
An identifier passed to an adapter so it can be recorded is also forwarded to the external service, bypassing the boundary that every outbound field must be declared and sanitized.
Fields that a shipped schema types as strings are only allow-listed by the hand-written validator, so values of any type pass validation and are forwarded outside the sanitizer.

A directory listing that keeps only plain directories misses symbolic links to directories, so a refusal keyed on that listing is skipped while a later existence check that follows links still finds the entry.

The end-to-end tests observe only a value the sanitizer computes itself, never what the external service actually receives, so wiring the raw input through instead of the sanitized input would go unnoticed.
A refusal test that checks only the exit status and an unanchored error substring also passes on an uncaught crash, so removing the error from the handled set goes unnoticed.
A static guard against a forbidden import searches for one textual form in one directory level, so other import forms or nested files evade it.
An outbound payload is rebuilt in configuration order after canonicalization, so the bytes sent no longer follow the contract's sorted-keys rule.
A reference usage line documents a narrower interface than the specification and the command's own help.
A shipped schema and the validator that claims to apply the same rules disagree on a range constraint, and the disagreement is neither documented nor tested.
A second copy of a usage synopsis was left showing one concrete invocation after the first copy was corrected to the specified interface.
The specification says a constraint is declared per item while the implementation declares it once for the whole configuration, and the change is not recorded as a decision.
A test named for a runtime property checks only the value of a constant, not that the code applies it, so removing the use leaves the suite green.
Every fixture pre-creates a directory the code is responsible for creating, so the creation path for the common first-run case is never exercised.
Fallback values for optional fields of an external record are never exercised because every fixture supplies those fields.
An entropy threshold set above the maximum entropy of a restricted alphabet makes the fallback scanner blind to every secret encoded in that alphabet.
Free text authored in a repository-controlled configuration file is forwarded to an external service without passing through the same credential scan as other outbound data.
A structured field returned by an external service is accepted after only a type check and persisted verbatim, with no bound on its shape or size.
A main-checkout lookup that compares a worktree path with the shared git directory misreads a worktree of a bare repository as the main checkout instead of refusing the layout.
A check-then-create sequence for a shared directory treats the already-exists error from a concurrent creator as a failure, so one of two simultaneous first runs loses its write.
A repository-controlled configuration file is read and parsed in full before any size limit applies, so an oversized file can exhaust memory before validation runs.
An identifier field in a repository-controlled configuration accepts any string and is forwarded to an external service, bypassing the credential scan applied to the configuration's other text.
A response size limit was compared only after the whole body had been buffered into memory, so the limit classified oversized replies but never bounded memory
An adapter mapped a reply field using a guessed meaning that no captured live response supported, so a wrong mapping would have produced plausible in-domain answers
An adapter split one logical request into several provider calls although the contract allows one call per run, which also made retries resend calls that had already succeeded
A contract test compared only the keys of a request against the live capture, so the values actually sent had never been shown to be accepted by the real service
Local request construction errors such as an invalid header value were caught as transport failures, retried, and recorded as a provider outage
A reply that omitted the resolved model identity was accepted, which silently skipped the pinned model mismatch check
Raw reply values that were not in the provider answer shape were passed through and could match the pack domain, producing a fabricated looking decision instead of a malformed error
A redirect test used a hand built response shape that the real fetch implementation never produces, so the production redirect path was untested
A test fed an endless stream to a size limited reader with no bound of its own, so a mutant that disabled the limit consumed memory without limit and froze the host

Widening a binary trust check to a privileged owner judged the followed target only, so a link anyone could plant toward a privileged program passed; trust must cover the link and its directory as well as the target.
A diagnostic explaining why no trusted binary ran was computed independently of the resolver, so a failure of a trusted binary that did run was misreported as a refusal of a different binary.
Tests exercised an extracted predicate with synthetic inputs but never the call site that uses it, so reverting the wiring would leave every test green.
Of several call sites changed to the same new message, only one was tested, and branches of the new message other than the first were never reached.
Documentation promised a stronger reporting behaviour than the code implements, describing every refused candidate where only the first is named.
A permission check applied file mode rules to a symbolic link, whose own mode bits are fixed and meaningless, so the exact install shape the change set out to accept was always refused.

A test fixture modelled a system call result in a shape the real call never returns, so the acceptance test passed while the real case failed; drive the real filesystem where a matching object exists.
A rejection test could not tell which of several conditions caused the refusal because they shared one reason, so removing any one condition left it green.

Trusting a binary because a privileged account owns it checked the file, its link and the immediate directory, but not the directories above them, any of which another account able to write could use to swap what runs.
A security check that consumes a computed list was tested only with hand-built lists, so the code that builds the list from the real filesystem could be gutted without any test failing.
A binary lookup that excluded one repository-controlled location still honoured relative search-path entries, which resolve inside the repository too.
One broad error handler treated a failure to inspect an existing candidate the same as no candidate at all, restoring the silence the change set out to remove.
The step that decides whether extra security inputs are gathered at all had no test that failed when it was skipped, because the only real case gave the same verdict either way.
A newly added refusal branch for unreadable inputs was unreachable from any test, so reverting it to the earlier silent skip left the suite green.
A refusal message interpolated a repository-influenced filesystem path verbatim into text the model reads, opening a small new channel from repository data into model context.
A fix for a runtime limit was tested only through an injected stub that echoes the option back, so nothing showed the real subprocess call now succeeds past the old limit
A subprocess failure reason preferred any stderr text over the error itself, so an unrelated warning on stderr could hide the real cause such as a buffer overflow or a signal
An output ceiling was set to a round number with no derivation from the worst-case payload it must hold, so the same overflow can return when the payload grows
A test asserted a constant against the same literal it was defined from, so it could not notice the value being too small

An error-classification branch handled a failure code the call could never produce, because the option that triggers it was never set, so the branch and its documentation described behaviour that cannot happen
Tests matched substrings independently where the contract promised an order and separator, and a test named for one failure shape exercised a different branch
A sizing test called the helper directly instead of the real caller, so the caller could stop using the sized helper with the test still green
A resource ceiling sized for one large call was applied through a shared helper to every call, so small probes lost their fail-fast bound
A bound test checked only part of the documented formula, so dropping the documented headroom would still pass
Error-classification tests built the platform error by hand, so drift in the real error shape would go unnoticed; one test must drive the real failure
